newsitem.title: USA: SGI probing over computer sale to Russia.
newsitem.headline: SGI probing over computer sale to Russia.

text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc said it has been working with the Department of Commerce to investigate whether high-powered computers shipped to a Russian laboratory are being used for nuclear arms testing.
The computer systems were bought by the Russian Scientific Research Institute for Technical Physics in 1996, the company said in a statement.

The institute had said the computers were for "modelling of earth-water pollution caused by extension of radioactive substances, for modelling of the Earth's atmosphere and for the research of atomic power plant safety," the company said.
Based on these representations, Silicon Graphics believed that this transaction did not require a licence from the Commerce Department, according to Silicon Graphics.
U.S. export laws dating back to the early days of the Cold War have limited exports of high-tech computers and other products that could be construed as munitions or used for military purposes.
"I am very concerned with this situation. Our reputation for integrity as a company is extremely important to us," said Silicon Graphics chairman and CEO Edward McCracken.
"These systems were shipped on the understanding that they would be used for environmental research," he said in a statement issued by the company's headquarters on Tuesday.
"It would be a major concern to us if Silicon Graphics systems have been diverted to end-uses that differ from the representations we received at the time of the shipment."

"In our review of the situation, it is apparent that errors in judgment were made by not asking the right questions prior to the sale and by not raising the issue to the top of our organisation for consideration," McCracken added.
"I take full responsibility for this situation," he said.
The company said it was cooperating with the Commerce Department to determine if the systems have been diverted for an inappropriate use.
"We take our obligations under the export laws seriously and believe that all our exports to end-users in Russia were made in compliance with applicable requirements," said McCracken.

Several high-profile cases of shipping computer equipment to the former Soviet Union in violation of export restrictions in the 1980s led to sanctions against companies by the U.S. government, although there has been a movement to liberalise export regulations since then.
